explanations.answer: No one alive is righteous before God
explanations.explanation: David, king of Israel, doesn't hand God a resume. He says, “…for no one alive is righteous before You.” That covers every living person, friend, and he doesn't leave himself out. I think it takes a big heart to walk into a prayer with no bragging at all.

explanations.answer: He has never done anything wrong
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. David never claims a spotless record, and the psalm says nothing like it. His reason is, “…no one alive is righteous before You.” He's asking for mercy, not pointing to a perfect track record.

explanations.answer: His enemies should be judged first
explanations.explanation: Enemies do show up in this psalm, but not in this verse. Here David gives one reason, and it has nothing to do with who goes first. He says, “…no one alive is righteous before You.” Nobody gets cut in line and nobody gets pointed at.

David says the enemy is making him dwell “in darkness like those long since dead.” That's a heavy line, and I think it hurts to read. I know a little about dark places, friend. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and nobody was going to hand me a flashlight. David puts it plainly in front of God, and that's a good place to put it.

A cave is a good guess, since David spent time in some in other stories, but this psalm doesn't mention one. What it says is darkness. The enemy has David “dwell in darkness like those long since dead.” The verse describes how it feels, and it never names a place on a map.

The wilderness is a fair guess, but it isn't in this verse. The word David uses is darkness. He says the enemy is “making me dwell in darkness like those long since dead.” The psalm never says where he is standing, only how heavy it is.

David says, “My spirit grows faint within me.” That's a spirit running low, like a mixer winding down with the batter still in the bowl. He doesn't hide it, either. He says out loud that his heart is dismayed.

Proud is a different feeling altogether, friend. The psalm says David's spirit grows faint, and his heart is dismayed. Nobody in this verse is puffing out their chest. He's telling God he's running low.

Bold sounds strong, and this verse is the opposite. David says, “My spirit grows faint within me; my heart is dismayed inside me.” He's being honest about how low he feels. Honest prayers are the kind I like best.

David says, “I consider the work of Your hands.” He also says he remembers the days of old and meditates on all God's works. When he's low, he looks back at what God has done. Good habit, friend, and cheaper than a therapy bill for your batter.

David has plenty of battles to look back on, but the psalm doesn't go there. He says, “I meditate on all Your works; I consider the work of Your hands.” His eyes are on what God has done. His own highlight reel stays in the drawer.

The psalm doesn't mention his youth at all, friend. When David remembers the days of old, he says, “I meditate on all Your works; I consider the work of Your hands.” His mind goes to God's works. That's the whole list.

Close, but the verse says something different. David doesn't say he's satisfied. He says, “my soul thirsts for You like a parched land.” That's a soul that's dry and reaching, not one sitting in a well-watered garden.

That's right, friend. David says, “I stretch out my hands to You; my soul thirsts for You like a parched land.” It's dry ground waiting on rain, not a well-watered garden. That's what I call an honest prayer.

explanations.answer: Those who descend to the Pit
explanations.explanation: David asks, “Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.” He's saying how much he needs God to answer. The Pit is a picture of the grave, and he does not want to go there. That's a serious line, so I'll keep my jokes in the oven for this one.

That picture shows up in other places in the Bible, but not in this psalm. Here David says, “Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.” Nothing in the verse mentions sheep. The picture is the Pit.

Grass that withers is a Bible picture, but it isn't in this verse. David says, “…or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.” That's the comparison he uses. The Pit is where he doesn't want to end up.

Yes, friend. David says, “Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul.” He's asking for directions, not just rescue. Smart man. I've never once regretted asking for directions, even with a mustache for a pointer.

It's true, friend. Right after he says he trusts God, David asks, “Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul.” He's asking God to show him the way, not just to fix things. Good ask.
David says, “I flee to You for refuge.” He's talking to the LORD, and that's where he runs. When the enemies close in, he runs straight to God. That's a smart place to run.
Other psalms have people looking at mountains, but this one doesn't. David says, “Deliver me from my enemies, O LORD; I flee to You for refuge.” His refuge isn't a place. It's the LORD Himself.
Friends are nice to have, friend, but this verse doesn't name them. David says, “I flee to You for refuge.” The “You” is the LORD. When he runs, he runs to God.
That's right. David prays, “May Your good Spirit lead me on level ground.” He's asking God's good Spirit to lead him. Level ground sounds good to me, friend. No tripping over the rolling pin.
It's true, friend. David prays, “May Your good Spirit lead me on level ground.” It comes right after he asks God to teach him to do His will. He wants to be led, not just left to figure it out.

explanations.answer: For the sake of God's name
explanations.explanation: David prays, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me.” His reason isn't his own comfort. It's God's name. I think that's a big deal, friend, since it points his prayer at God and not at himself.

explanations.answer: For the sake of his family
explanations.explanation: David's family doesn't come up anywhere in this psalm. What he says is, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me.” The reason is God's name. Nobody else is on the guest list for this one.

explanations.answer: For the sake of his army
explanations.explanation: David was a king, so an army is a reasonable guess. This psalm never brings one up, though. He prays, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me.” His reason is God's name.

David prays, “And in Your loving devotion, cut off my enemies.” He's asking God to do it, and he asks it in God's loving devotion. This is a heavy line, so I'm not joking about it. He ends by saying, “for I am Your servant.”

Forgive is a gentle word, friend, but it isn't the one David uses. His words are, “And in Your loving devotion, cut off my enemies.” It's a hard line to read, and the psalm doesn't soften it. He closes by saying, “for I am Your servant.”

Bless would make this a different prayer. David actually says, “And in Your loving devotion, cut off my enemies.” That's a heavy line, and the psalm leaves it as it is. He ends by saying, “for I am Your servant.”
